documents.abstract: Fiqh instruction in many Islamic schools remains predominantly teacher-centered, rendering it less effective for engaging the contemporary digital generation that demands active, contextual, and exploratory learning experiences. The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into the Inquiry Learning model offers a strategic pedagogical innovation to enhance instructional quality while maintaining the teacher's vital role as a facilitator. This study aims to describe the integration of AI across each stage of Inquiry Learning in Fiqh instruction at SMP IT Mutiara Ilmu Sokaraja, Banyumas Regency. Employing a descriptive qualitative approach with a field research design, data were gathered through classroom observations, in-depth interviews with the principal, the Fiqh teacher, and students, alongside instructional documentation review. Data analysis followed the Miles and Huberman interactive model, complemented by source and method triangulation to ensure data trustworthiness. The findings reveal that AI was systematically integrated into problem identification, data collection, data analysis, and conclusion synthesis through the utilization of ChatGPT, Perplexity AI, Google Gemini, and NotebookLM. AI was most heavily utilized during the data gathering and comparative analysis phases, while the teacher retained an indispensable role as a facilitator, ethical guide, and legal validator. These insights underscore that the successful implementation of AI in Islamic jurisprudence education relies fundamentally on the teacher's pedagogical competence to thoughtfully scaffold AI tools within an inquiry framework to cultivate critical thinking. ABSTRAK Pembelajaran Fiqih di banyak sekolah masih didominasi metode konvensional yang berpusat pada guru sehingga kurang mampu mengakomodasi karakteristik generasi digital yang membutuhkan pembelajaran aktif, kontekstual, dan berbasis eksplorasi. Integrasi Artificial Intelligence (AI) dalam model Inquiry Learning menjadi salah satu inovasi strategis yang berpotensi mentransformasi kualitas pembelajaran tanpa mengesampingkan peran guru sebagai fasilitator utama. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk mendeskripsikan integrasi AI pada setiap tahapan Inquiry Learning dalam pembelajaran Fiqih di SMP IT Mutiara Ilmu Sokaraja, Kabupaten Banyumas. Pendekatan penelitian yang digunakan adalah kualitatif deskriptif dengan jenis studi lapangan (field research). Data diperoleh melalui observasi kelas, wawancara mendalam bersama kepala sekolah, guru Fiqih, dan siswa, serta telaah dokumentasi perangkat ajar. Analisis data dilakukan menggunakan model interaktif Miles dan Huberman, sedangkan keabsahan data diuji melalui triangulasi sumber dan triangulasi teknik. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa AI diintegrasikan secara proporsional pada tahap identifikasi masalah, pengumpulan data, analisis data, serta penarikan kesimpulan dan penyajian hasil dengan memanfaatkan platform ChatGPT, Perplexity AI, Google Gemini, dan NotebookLM. Pemanfaatan AI paling dominan terdapat pada tahap pengumpulan dan analisis data, sementara guru tetap memegang kendali sentral sebagai fasilitator, pengarah etika digital, dan validator hukum syariat. Temuan ini menegaskan bahwa keberhasilan integrasi teknologi dalam pembelajaran Fiqih sangat bergantung pada kompetensi pedagogis guru dalam merajut teknologi AI secara tepat ke dalam sintaks inkuiri yang berorientasi pada nalar kritis siswa.

This chapter examines how political institutions in China function as mechanisms of authoritarian adaptation rather than as checks on state power. It argues that the resilience of the Chinese party-state lies not in institutional liberalisation, but in the CCP&s;s ability to continuously reorganise, coordinate and recalibrate institutions in ways that preserve centralised political control while responding pragmatically to social, economic and geopolitical pressures. Using a political-technology “stack” lens, the chapter analyses how governance operates across interacting layers of discourse, bureaucracy, data, platforms and coercion, demonstrating that authority in China emerges from the coordinated functioning of an integrated party-state system rather than from isolated institutions. It explores key institutional arenas, including the National People&s;s Congress, the Two Sessions, the People&s;s Liberation Army, civil society governance and economic reform, highlighting how mechanisms such as consultative authoritarianism, stability maintenance, party-led military control and selective incorporation of NGOs contribute to regime durability. The chapter also traces the historical evolution of institutional adaptation from the reform era to the Xi Jinping period, examining how market reforms, Special Economic Zones and “socialism with Chinese characteristics” enabled economic transformation without political liberalisation. Through simulations, artificial intelligence (AI) check exercises and comparative analysis, the chapter encourages students to critically assess how authoritarian systems evolve, manage participation and sustain legitimacy under conditions of rapid social change and global uncertainty.

The rapid digital transformation of higher education and legal practice, together with the internationalization of legal services and the growing integration of artificial intelligence into professional activities, have fundamentally reshaped the requirements for preparing future lawyers. In this context, professional English competence extends beyond language proficiency to encompass the ability to operate effectively in multilingual, technology-enhanced, and intercultural legal environments. The purpose of the study is to theoretically develop and substantiate an integrative model to foster the professional English competence of future lawyers through Legal English in digitally enhanced legal education. The proposed model is grounded in competency-based, communicative, interdisciplinary, and learner-centred approaches while incorporating digital pedagogy, AI-supported learning, and professional legal communication. The study employs theoretical methods, including comparative analysis, conceptual synthesis, modelling, and systematization of contemporary ESP approaches. Particular attention is devoted to authentic legal discourse, casebased learning, Moot Court simulations, digital legal resources, and generative artificial intelligence as tools that support professional language development, academic integrity, and the critical evaluation of AI-generated content. The scientific novelty lies in the development of an integrative pedagogical model that conceptualizes professional English competence as a multidimensional construction comprising motivational-professional, legal-linguistic, professional-communicative, digital-AI, and reflectivedevelopmental components. The model positions Legal English as a strategic instrument for developing professional communication, legal reasoning, digital competence, and international professional mobility. The practical significance of the model lies in its applicability to curriculum design, Legal English syllabi, ESP course development, digital learning environments and professional training for future lawyers. It also supports alignment with international professional requirements and preparation for Legal English assessment frameworks such as TOLES.

Traditional reinforced concrete (RC) design has historically relied on time-consuming, iterative manual calculations to ensure structural safety. While effective for maintaining security, this method often hampers efficiency and innovation. Consequently, it has struggled to fully meet modern demands for sustainable and optimized construction. These approaches rely heavily on conservative assumptions, standardized material properties, and empirical rules. As a result, they lead to time-intensive design cycles, over-reinforced sections, and suboptimal outcomes in complex or non-standard scenarios. The inherent limitations in exploring high-dimensional design spaces and integrating multi-objective criteria (e.g., cost, durability, and environmental impact) restrict the potential for performance-based, adaptive, and resource-efficient structures. This chapter introduces artificial intelligence (AI)-driven design and optimization as a transformative paradigm shift. With the help of machine learning (ML), deep neural networks, genetic algorithms, and hybrid computational frameworks, it enables data-driven, predictive, and highly optimized RC systems. By automating generative design, topology optimization, and lifecycle performance forecasting, AI produces intelligent concrete structures that are stronger, lighter, and more sustainable. Despite its promise, the chapter also reviews key challenges such as data scarcity, interpretability of AI models, computational costs, regulatory compliance, and ethical concerns, underscoring the need for explainable AI and human–AI collaboration. Real-world case studies and meta-analyses highlight measurable environmental and economic benefits, advocating AI as a transformative paradigm for future sustainable construction. The chapter closes by calling for interdisciplinary efforts to advance reliable, transparent, and equitable AI adoption in structural engineering.

As artificial intelligence systems evolve from analytical tools into autonomous agents capable of interacting directly with financial markets, a new governance problem emerges: the same system may generate an investment decision, determine whether its own risk is acceptable, and execute the resulting transaction. This paper introduces Interactive Governance, a separation-of-powers architecture for autonomous financial agents built around a simple principle: AI can propose. Governance can authorize. Execution can execute. No component should control all three. The framework separates three distinct authorities: investment decision-making, independent authorization, and brokerage execution. It is implemented and examined through ALEX, an experimental autonomous investment architecture combining a transparent portfolio decision engine with an independently deployed execution system connected to Interactive Brokers. The implementation includes physical separation between decision and execution environments, target-state portfolio reconciliation, up to 18 deterministic pre-trade governance checks, fail-closed defaults, protocol locking, audit preservation, execution-state controls, market-session validation, liquidity and concentration limits, and independent human emergency authority. The paper also examines evidence from the ALEX Fund pilot, including unsuccessful investment outcomes, not as evidence of superior investment performance but as an empirical motivation for separating investment conviction from final risk authority. Interactive Governance is positioned as the action layer of the broader ALEX cognitive architecture, extending governance from belief formation and uncertainty management into external financial action. The resulting framework distinguishes between cognitive autonomy and operational authority and argues that increasingly capable AI systems require stronger, rather than weaker, separation between reasoning, authorization, and execution. The central conclusion is that the primary challenge in autonomous finance is no longer enabling AI to trade. It is designing systems in which artificial intelligence can be wrong without possessing the unrestricted authority to amplify its own error. The
