documents.abstract: Electrocardiography (ECG) records the electrical activity of the heart, aiding diagnosis by detecting abnormalities in cardiac function. ECG foundation models have demonstrated promising results, but are limited by a reliance on ECG interpretation reports as their sole supervision. Because interpretation reports only capture the subset of waveform information routinely recognized by clinicians, this constrains representation learning to overlook the broader diagnostic signals present in ECG. We introduce a new ECG foundation model --- MS-ECG-FM --- that is trained through contrastive alignment to multiple distinct clinical note types, including ECG, echocardiography, radiology, and discharge reports. We evaluate MS-ECG-FM on an extended set of ECG detection benchmarks, showing that it comprehensively outperforms existing methods on the full span of conditions that ECG can detect, including in reduced-lead configurations. Different reports improve representations for different diagnostic domains, while multi-source alignment captures their complementary information and produces consistently strong representations across clinically diverse tasks.

Achieving compositional concept generalization (CoCoGen), the ability to understand novel situations by recombining learned primitives, remains a fundamental challenge in artificial intelligence. Compositional semantic models such as Compositional Distributional Semantics (DisCoCat) offer solutions by generalising vectors to tensors, but suffer from scaling bottlenecks when learning the tensors. Mapping DisCoCat onto Variational Quantum Circuits (VQCs) resolves this limitation for text, yet the methodology has not been expanded to multimodal situations such as the ones involved in CoCoGen. This paper introduces Mu-DisCoCat: a multimodal variational quantum learning framework for DisCoCat that achieves CoCoGen. The framework first learns stable object representations from single-object image-text pairs, then fixes these and uses them to learn the relations between them in multi-object situations. In classical simulations, the model used Uhlmann state fidelity to compute the overlap between the multimodal circuit representations and achieved higher relational OOD accuracy than the evaluated CLIP baseline. Its deployment was evaluated using the destructive SWAP test across noisy quantum emulators, including a range of IBM fake backends, IQM FakeAphrodite, and the IBM Marrakesh quantum processor. Despite real-world device noise, the hardware-executed models maintained a strong positive correlation with simulated fidelities, reliably distinguishing unseen similar and dissimilar pairs. Our work establishes a framework for executing CoCoGen on VQCs, demonstrating a viable use case for near-term quantum hardware.

Multi-label topic assignment for user-generated content (UGC) -- including product reviews and buyer-seller conversations -- poses unique scalability challenges in large-scale e-commerce due to informal language, extreme label sparsity, and rapidly evolving taxonomies. While utilizing Large Language Models (LLMs) as labeling oracles to distill ground-truth data has emerged as an industry standard to bypass prohibitive manual annotation costs, determining the optimal, low-latency architecture for the resulting student models remains an open challenge. To address this, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation across Small Language Model (SLM) parameter scales (1B, 4B, and 8B) and architectural paradigms (causal generative versus bidirectional discriminative). Comparing generative text-to-label classifiers against discriminative baselines (DeBERTa-V3 and ModernBERT), our analysis reveals a crucial data-dependent trade-off: while discriminative models outperform ultra-lightweight generative models on structured product reviews, even the smallest 1B generative model surpasses discriminative baselines on complex, multi-turn conversational data. Furthermore, generative models maintain robust performance under massive label-set expansion (up to 112 topics) and severe long-tail distributions, whereas discriminative baselines suffer a 35% drop in Macro-F1 at scale. Finally, we detail the successful production deployment of these optimized models across both product review and conversational domains, demonstrating strict latency compliance and tangible business impact at a global marketplace scale.

Substance Use Disorder (SUD) counseling requires patient responses that reflect underlying cognitive states such as beliefs, coping strategies, and readiness for change. Although large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent text, they often fail to produce cognitively coherent and clinically realistic patient behavior, especially under ethical and data-scarce clinical settings. Moreover, deploying frontier-scale LLMs in healthcare applications presents practical challenges including high computational cost, latency, privacy concerns, and limited deployability in resource-constrained environments, motivating the need for cognitively aligned small language models (SLMs). We propose a cognitively grounded framework for SUD patient dialogue generation that explicitly models and aligns latent cognitive components with patient histories and counselor questions. Our pipeline consists of two stages: cognitive component detection and cognitive component-aligned dialogue generation. To enable effective learning with smaller models, we combine knowledge distillation from high-capacity teacher models, preference optimization from human-annotations, and attention-guided reward shaping. Extensive evaluations using automatic scores like BERTScore, ROUGE, METEOR and BLEU, and LLM-as-judge hit-metrics against both human and teacher-model references show that cognitively informed fine-tuning substantially improves cognitive realization and alignment over a generic instruction-tuned baselines and mental health domain specific SLMs, with particularly strong gains for open-ended cognitive components.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Generative AI chatbots are increasingly used for health information, but their performance in safety-sensitive sudden cardiac death (SCD) consultation remains insufficiently characterized. This study evaluated six publicly accessible chatbots on SCD-related public questions involving symptom triage, emergency response, CPR/AED use, inherited risk, myocarditis-related concerns, return to exercise, screening, and ICD decision-making. This cross-sectional, comparative, text-level study evaluated ChatGPT Plus 5.5 thinking, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Microsoft Copilot smart, DeepSeek-V4-pro, Doubao, and Perplexity. A standardized set of 56 SCD-related public consultation questions was developed from Google Trends, online forums, public question-answer platforms, clinical guidelines, expert consensus statements, systematic reviews, and qualitative interviews. Each question was submitted once to each chatbot between May 10 and May 16, 2026, yielding 336 model-response items. Five blinded senior cardiology raters assessed safety, accuracy, empathy, DISCERN, EQIP, JAMA benchmark criteria, and GQS. Readability was calculated using six formula-based indices. Between-model comparisons were performed using Cochran’s Q test and Friedman tests, with Kendall’s W reported as the effect size. Responses containing potential safety concerns were additionally examined qualitatively. Inter-rater agreement was high across all manually assessed metrics, with Fleiss’ kappa of 0.856 for Safety and ICC values ranging from 0.801 to 0.887 for other domains. Safe responses predominated across all models, although responses containing potential safety concerns occurred in every chatbot. ChatGPT Plus 5.5 thinking and Perplexity had the highest observed safety proportions during this query window, whereas Doubao had the lowest. Qualitative analysis identified recurrent concerns involving delayed emergency activation for chest pain, syncope, or post-viral symptoms; over-reassurance about prevention; fixed return-to-exercise timelines after infection or COVID-19; pulse-check instructions that could delay CPR; and oversimplified screening, electrolyte, or ICD-related advice. Most flagged responses contained a single potential safety concern. The qualitative severity distribution was concentrated in low and low-to-moderate concerns, whereas higher-severity concerns were less frequent. Accuracy differed significantly across models ( P < 0.001; Kendall’s W = 0.864), with ChatGPT Plus 5.5 thinking, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Microsoft Copilot smart, DeepSeek-V4-pro, and Perplexity achieving similar median scores and Doubao performing lower. Empathy also differed significantly ( P < 0.001; Kendall’s W = 0.531), with DeepSeek-V4-pro having the highest observed score. Significant differences were observed for DISCERN, EQIP, JAMA, GQS, and all readability indices (all P < 0.001). Within this dataset, DeepSeek-V4-pro had the highest DISCERN and EQIP scores and the most favorable readability profile, Gemini 3.5 Flash showed comparable EQIP performance, and Microsoft Copilot smart had the highest JAMA score. However, transparency remained limited overall, and all models produced responses with relatively high reading-grade requirements. In this multidimensional evaluation of six generative AI chatbots for SCD-related public consultation, most responses were safe and clinically relevant, but potential safety concerns occurred across all models. Important limitations involved emergency escalation, CPR/AED guidance, return-to-exercise advice, individualized risk interpretation, transparency, and readability. These tools may support general SCD education, but they should not replace emergency medical services or clinician assessment. Because each question was sampled once during a defined week and all prompts were submitted in English through public interfaces accessed in China, the findings should be interpreted as a time-, language-, and access-specific snapshot rather than a stable ranking of the underlying models. Future development should prioritize evidence-linked content, clear red-flag escalation, plain-language communication, and ongoing expert review.

documents.abstract: Abstract Callous-unemotional (CU) traits, defined by deficient empathy and remorse, characterize a distinct subgroup of antisocial individuals with more severe behavioral problems and unique affective profiles. Two processes implicated in the development of CU traits are hyporeactivity to and inaccurate recognition of others’ emotions. Although many studies link CU traits to emotional processing deficits, findings have been inconsistent across age and sex. We conducted multilevel meta-analyses of emotional reactivity and recognition, accounting for age and sex as moderators, to clarify these discrepancies. A four-level meta-analysis indicated CU traits were negatively associated with emotional reactivity to both broad emotional stimuli ( r = − .23, p < .0001; k = 106, n ES = 402) and distress-specific stimuli ( r = − .22, p < .0001; k = 84, n ES = 234), with no moderation by age or sex. Similarly, a three-level meta-analysis showed CU traits were negatively associated with recognition accuracy for both broad facial emotions ( r = − .09, p < .0001; k = 97, n ES = 437) and distress (e.g., fear, sadness; r = − .10, p < .0001; k = 60, n ES = 140). Sample age moderated broad ( r = .003, p = .01) and distress ( r = .004, p = .04) recognition deficits, such that effects diminished with sample age. These results are consistent with theoretical models proposing emotional hyporeactivity represents a developmentally stable correlate of CU traits that may reduce intrinsic motivation for emotion recognition early in development. Such developmental changes also have implications for improving treatments for individuals with elevated CU traits.

Gastric adenocarcinoma (GA) is a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, and accurate histopathological subtype classification from whole-slide images (WSIs) is essential for effective treatment planning. While multimodal approaches that integrate pathology report text with WSIs can improve classification, existing methods often depend on computationally expensive transformer architectures and large language models. We propose a multimodal knowledge distillation (MKD) framework that combines a pretrained WSI image encoder and a clinical text encoder using Low-Rank Multimodal Fusion (LMF) to efficiently model cross-modal interactions during training. Each WSI is represented as a bag of patches paired with a slide-level diagnostic caption. The teacher model learns fused image-text representations for subtype classification, while the student model distills this knowledge to enable accurate image-only inference. We evaluate our method on the PatchGastric benchmark dataset and achieve at least 3.35% higher mean accuracy than state-of-the-art approaches, without relying on transformer-based fusion, multi-task learning, or large language models. The source code is available at https://github.com/helomelo1/MKD-LMF.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: Natural-language access to RDF knowledge graphs is a core Semantic Web ambition. Large language models (LLMs) have advanced Text-to-SPARQL, yet on unfamiliar graphs they often generate valid queries that misrepresent the populated data model. QRAKEN is a training-free, ontology-agnostic neurosymbolic pipeline grounding generation in empirical graph evidence rather than schema expectations. An offline distiller produces TTQL, a compact description of populated multi-hop patterns, conditional frequencies and path-conditioned literal examples, plus a class-property co-occurrence matrix. Online, TTQL guides the LLM, while deterministic syntax, vocabulary and data-model checks provide diagnostics for iterative refinement. On CK25 (First International Text2SPARQL Challenge), under matched-condition recomputation on a QLever snapshot, QRAKEN achieves strict F1 of 0.643 $\pm$ 0.026 with GPT-4.1 mini and 0.652 $\pm$ 0.012 with GPT-5.4: relative gains of 30% and 32% over the strongest recomputed participant, outperforming systems using the same base model family. Ablations identify TTQL patterns as the dominant driver (+0.31 strict F1 over a shape-only baseline); the refinement loop provides a cheap safety net, rejecting triple patterns unsupported by the co-occurrence matrix. Compared with auto-derived SHACL, TTQL yields 64% higher strict F1, supporting the value of empirical patterns beyond schema exposure. With two local 35B 4-bit open-weight models at zero marginal cost, the same pipeline matches the strongest recomputed participant, and TTQL advantages over shape-only and SHACL baselines persist. Results on a single, relatively small benchmark provide an initial empirical signal; monolithic TTQL injection on very open cross-domain graphs remains the main limitation.

NeST: Neuron-Selective Tuning for Efficient Safety Alignment A lightweight and structure-aware safety alignment framework that selectively adapts safety-relevant neurons to strengthen refusal behavior while preserving the model's general capabilities. 🚀 Overview Safety alignment is essential for reliable deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs), but existing approaches often require costly model-wide fine-tuning or introduce additional inference-time overhead. Parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA improve efficiency but can provide inconsistent safety gains, while intervention-based methods do not directly shape the model's internal safety representations. NeST addresses these limitations by selectively tuning a small set of safety-relevant neurons while freezing the rest of the model. NeST groups functionally coherent safety neurons into clusters and learns shared updates within each cluster, enabling targeted, stable, and efficient safety adaptation. We evaluate NeST across 14 open-weight LLMs spanning multiple model families and sizes, achieving: 1.1% average ASR, down from 44.5%, corresponding to a 97.5% reduction in unsafe generations. 5,800× fewer trainable parameters than full fine-tuning and 3× fewer than the lowest-rank LoRA baseline. 1.1% average ASR on multimodal models, down from 55.3% across text, image, and reasoning-augmented settings. 0.8% average ASR on downstream-adapted models, down from 53.8%, demonstrating effective post-hoc safety restoration. 🧪 Key Contributions Neuron-Selective Tuning for lightweight, post-hoc safety alignment by modifying only safety-relevant neurons while freezing the remainder of the model. Cluster-Based Safety Adaptation that groups safety neurons by activation similarity and learns shared updates within each cluster for structured and stable refusal behavior. Extensive Evaluation across 14 open-weight LLMs, showing strong safety robustness with substantially fewer trainable parameters while preserving core reasoning and knowledge capabilities. Multimodal Safety Alignment across text-only, image-only, and reasoning-augmented generation, demonstrating robust safety improvements across diverse input modalities. Post-Hoc Downstream Hardening by transferring safety-relevant neuron clusters from base models to downstream variants, efficiently restoring safety after task-specific fine-tuning.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Neurodivergent students have been largely overlooked in research examining student experiences with generative AI (GenAI) in higher education, creating critical knowledge gaps about inclusive educational technology use. This sequential multi-method qualitative study examined how neurodivergent students (NDS) and neurotypical students (NTS) interact with and experience GenAI in academic contexts. Using a sequential design, we employed a virtual revisit think-aloud protocol with 24 university students (12 NDS, 12 NTS) completing an academic task using Microsoft Copilot, followed by focus groups with 14 participants (7 NDS, 7 NTS) to contextualise these task-based behaviours through broader GenAI perceptions. A neurodivergent research advisory board co-designed all procedures. Three themes emerged: approaching the task efficiently, evaluating and refining output, and maintaining academic integrity. While both groups demonstrated strategic GenAI use, neurodivergent participants in this sample explicitly described their cognitive processing needs, using GenAI to manage energy, and humanising some AI interactions. In the neurodivergent focus group, students described GenAI as essential scaffolding for managing academic demands, though this created complex tensions around authenticity and over-reliance. Interface design challenges seemed to particularly disadvantage users with executive function differences. As institutions rapidly integrate these technologies, inclusive design principles and empirical evidence regarding diverse student needs are essential to ensure equitable access to AI-supported education.

Artificial intelligence has experienced tremendous success over the years. This is despite the fact that conventional deep learning models have shortcomings when it comes to matters of energy efficiency, adaptability, temporal computation, and their alignment with biological processes. The human brain, on the other hand, demonstrates highly efficient, strong, and adaptive intelligence processes via event-driven neural communication and local learning processes. There has since been a growing focus on the concept of neuromorphic intelligence. This involves the use of biological processes for intelligence AI models. This paper presents a systematically arranged review of neuromorphic intelligence and its approaches using biological brain mechanisms such as spiking neural communication, neural coding schemes, and synaptic plasticity. Here, advanced biologically inspired models such as spiking neural networks would be examined with respect to their learning procedures, characteristics, and advantages over artificial neural networks. In order to clearly define the abovementioned ideas, a simple proof-of-concept technique involving the implementation of spiking neural networks with spike computing and biologically inspired learning would be depicted. Finally, this paper considers existing difficulties involved in biologically inspired scaling mechanisms for scalable AI systems, along with the future directions of researching neuromorphic intelligence. Through the integration of knowledge gained from neuroscience and AI, this paper can offer a robust basis for researchers seeking brain-inspired solutions for developments involving the next generation of intelligence.

This chapter examines the transformation of higher education governance and institutional decision-making driven by broad-based digitalisation. As universities evolve from traditionally bureaucratic institutions into data-driven digital organisations, their governing bodies must deal with a substantially new set of sociotechnical, ethical, and operational conditions. Drawing on algorithmic governance concepts and distributed organisation theory, the chapter evaluates the shift from deliberative administration based on committees and dialogue to near real-time oversight informed by data. Key themes addressed include the integration of business intelligence dashboards into strategic planning, the institutional opportunities as well as the risks and practical difficulties of distributed internal crowdsourcing and online participatory budgeting, and the growing complexity of regulatory compliance under frameworks like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Furthermore, the chapter positions cybersecurity and digital risk management as central governance concerns requiring active and visible representation on university boards. Expanding beyond domestic borders, the chapter examines the cross-jurisdictional challenges that global distance education creates for institutional leadership, requiring governance structures to navigate conflicting privacy laws across countries, regional systems of internet censorship, and inequalities in infrastructure. The chapter closes by examining the institutional tensions between technocratic forms of managerialism, operational efficiency, and the preservation of central academic values, collegial traditions, and democratic accountability in the current digital era.

An agentic system issues several structurally different kinds of LLM calls. It routes intent, classifies actions, grounds language in a device registry, plans multi-agent pipelines and writes the Python code those pipelines run. The difficulty of these call sites varies by an order of magnitude, yet in practice a single model, chosen for the hardest site, serves all of them. In this work, we evaluate 9 models from 0.8B to a frontier hosted model across the five call sites of a deployed open-source home-automation framework (Wactorz), using its unmodified production prompts and two real Home Assistant installations (280 cases, 2520 scored calls). We find that capability is not ordered the same way at every site, and that larger models are not uniformly better: one 4B model is worse than its 2B sibling at grounded actuation. Paired testing shows the best local model to be statistically indistinguishable from both hosted models at four of five sites. Only code generation separates them, against a small hosted model (p = 0.039) as well as a frontier one (p = 0.002). Aggregate accuracy also hides a safety failure specific to actuation, where small models resolve the accuracy/refusal trade-off in degenerate ways: one model (Gemma4 E2B) actuates on 87.2% of requests for devices the site does not own, while another refuses every request it receives. Routing each site to its best local model reaches 91.8% against 95.4% at no per-call cost. In a live deployment judged by a user, hosting only the two generative sites matches hosting everything (39/43 against 39/43) for 28% of the spend, and the actuation gap the benchmark predicted appears as exactly one case in twenty-six. Benchmark, harness and all records are released at https://github.com/waldiez/slm-callsite-eval.

Abstract This study examines one-year changes in students’ intrinsic motivational orientation towards mathematics and whether these changes are gendered. Drawing on Swedish data from the TIMSS 2023 Longitudinal Study, we analysed two student cohorts, followed from Grade 4 to Grade 5 and from Grade 8 to Grade 9. Building on a theoretical recoding of TIMSS affective questionnaire items, intrinsic motivation was analysed as an overarching category, with cognitive and emotional motivation treated as subcategories. Mean change analyses and categorical change analyses were used to examine both average change and the proportions of students who decreased, remained stable, or increased. The younger cohort reported more positive orientations than the older cohort but declined over the year, while the older cohort started lower and showed weak positive change or stabilisation. Emotional motivation showed more variability than cognitive motivation, and the two subcategories did not move in identical ways. Gender differences in change were small: girls in the younger group were more likely to decrease, especially emotionally, but there were no significant differences in the older group. Findings suggest that mathematics-related affective development is uneven and dimension-specific rather than a simple decline, with gender differences more visible in the younger cohort than in the older cohort.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools are widely used to support decision making in tasks and domains where no immediate performance feedback is available. In these settings, users cannot learn to adjust their reliance behavior over time through trial and error. However, little is known about how novice users calibrate reliance on AI when external feedback is unavailable, or whether AI explanations can support calibration in its absence. We introduce reliance calibration as an organizing construct for studying how novice users dynamically adjust reliance behavior, and examine how AI explanations and meta-cognitive self-assessment shape it. Through a between-subjects study with 110 participants completing a clinical entity extraction task with AI assistance and limited performance feedback, we observe that novice users exhibit systematic drift toward over-reliance in the presence of explanations, while higher self-reported task understanding is associated with more selective reliance behavior. These results extend reliance calibration research into human-AI collaboration contexts without real-time performance signals and present actionable guidelines on designing AI tools that must support appropriate reliance in these settings.

documents.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Occupational hazards (OH) in healthcare facilities are common, with 1 in 10 healthcare workers experiencing a hazard each year. These hazards can be either biological, chemical, ergonomic, or radiation. Despite their occurrence, reporting of these hazards remains limited, with very little information available, especially from healthcare facilities. Also, there is limited information on incident reporting systems (IRSs), which can help capture, track, and monitor the occurrence of these hazards within health facilities. The absence of these systems results in inaccurate and incomplete reporting and fragmented data, hindering the implementation of effective occupational safety measures in hospitals. This review will explore the extent and nature of information available on occupational hazard incident reporting systems in Sub-Saharan Africa. METHODS: The review will be conducted using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology of scoping reviews and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). A robust search strategy shall be conducted in different scientific databases, including PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science, guided by the Population, Concept, and Context framework. Studies describing incident reporting systems shall be considered in this review. The search results will be collated and uploaded to Covidence, where duplicates will be removed and titles and abstracts screened. Search and screening of studies have not yet commenced. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION: Occupational health and safety are vital to the functioning of healthcare facilities because they promote well-being and protect both patients and healthcare workers. It is vital to ensure accurate and robust IRS are in place, especially given the occurrence of occupational hazards across hospital wards. These IRS will help with surveillance and the identification of epidemiological trends in OH among health workers. PROTOCOL REGISTRATION: The protocol has not been registered.

documents.abstract: In pediatrics, drugs require specific study in children rather than being prescribed based on data extrapolated from adults. Historically, this requirement was hindered by various challenges, resulting in widespread off-label drug use. The extent of such use has been extensively investigated, and new regulations in the US and Europe came into force. We conducted a narrative review addressing the epidemiology, associated risks, and regulatory implications of off-label drug use. This involved performing a targeted PubMed search and synthesizing relevant review articles and policy guidelines. The included studies, despite being informative, showed substantial heterogeneity, limiting the comparability and interpretability of their findings. Particularly, quantitative evidence regarding associated risks remains scarce. In addition to risks to patients, liability represents an important concern. Although regulatory policies vary between countries, the level of supporting evidence and accepted standards of practice are consistently central considerations. Future efforts should therefore focus on using available data to inform individual treatment decisions, ensuring this knowledge is accessible to prescribers, and addressing areas where evidence is particularly limited and patient safety is most compromised. Artificial intelligence and modeling may facilitate evidence generation and improve clinical-trial efficiency. Nevertheless, these approaches should complement, not replace, research conducted directly in pediatric patients.

"Developments in artificial intelligence and digitalization have helped new and advanced approaches grow and become more common in educational measurement and evaluation. In this chapter, we first explain the theoretical basis of Computerized Adaptive Testing (CAT) and Multistage Testing (MST). This includes components such as the entry rule, the item selection method, ability estimation, likelihood and classical Bayesian approaches, robust estimators, and termination rules. We also cover MST-specific design elements such as panel design, module length, and routing conditions. Using examples from international tests such as GRE, PISA, and SAT, we show clearly how these theoretical design choices are put into practice in real testing systems. The chapter also examines Automatic Item Generation (AIG), which was developed to solve the time, cost, and subjectivity limitations of traditional item writing. Model-based, artificial intelligence–based, and hybrid (bridge) approaches are presented together with their stages and their strengths and limitations, and they are illustrated through examples of applications in Turkish. In addition to the scalability that artificial intelligence and large language models offer, ethical risks such as hallucination, inconsistency, bias, copyright, and data security are discussed, and the importance of the ""augmented intelligence"" approach based on human–artificial intelligence collaboration is highlighted. Finally, the chapter deals with test equating, which aims to make scores from different test forms that measure the same construct comparable. It explains the basic concepts of equating, its conditions (symmetry, measuring the same construct, equal reliability, equity, observed score equity, and group invariance), and the data collection designs (random groups, single group, counterbalanced group, and common item/common variable in non-equivalent groups). Equating methods based on Classical Test Theory and Item Response Theory, as well as the types of equating error, are presented together with international and national application examples."

This chapter examines the theoretical foundations of psychological attributes targeted for measurement, their role in educational measurement and assessment, and the ways in which they are conceptualized within contemporary psychometric approaches. It begins by explaining that psychological attributes are conceptualized in psychometrics as latent constructs that cannot be observed directly but can be measured indirectly through behavioral indicators using scores obtained from measurement instruments supported by strong validity and reliability evidence. The chapter then discusses the principal approaches to measuring cognitive, affective, and psychomotor attributes. Within the cognitive domain, it addresses educational taxonomies, types of knowledge, and the concepts of skills and competencies. Within the affective domain, it examines attitudes, interests, motivation, self-efficacy, personality, and anxiety. Within the psychomotor domain, it focuses on performance-based observation and skill assessment. The chapter further reviews the historical development of intelligence and ability assessment, the assessment of school learning, the influence of cultural context on the interpretation of assessment results, and the opportunities created by digitalization and artificial intelligence-supported assessment practices. Finally, it presents a conceptual framework for the responsible use of assessment results in individual and societal decision-making by emphasizing the importance of validity, reliability, fairness, ethics, and interpretability in the measurement of psychological attributes.

The biomedical literature contains a vast collection of omics studies, yet most published data remain functionally inaccessible for computational reuse. When raw data are deposited in public repositories, essential information for reproducing reported results is dispersed across main text, supplementary files, and code repositories, and in the rarer cases where intermediate data (e.g. protein abundance files) are shared, their location is irregular. Here we present an agentic framework for the agent-supported retrieval, reanalysis, and synthesis of published omics data. The system employs large language model (LLM) agents with access to tools for fetching omics studies, extracting article metadata, identifying and downloading published data, executing containerized quantification pipelines, and synthesizing results across studies. Applied at corpus scale, the pipeline catalogued dataset references across thousands of PubMed Central articles; we report these as descriptive system outputs rather than as a validated measure of extraction accuracy. Using model context protocol (MCP) servers to expose containerized analysis tools, the agents retrieved and re-quantified data in five end-to-end reanalyses spanning data-dependent and data-independent proteomics and bulk RNA-seq. All five reanalyses completed, each with documented human guidance and workflow accommodations, and reproduced the authors' deposited abundances with high per-sample correlation (0.85-0.997) and strongly concordant differentially expressed features (fold-change Spearman 0.88-0.91), with no direction reversals among features called differentially expressed in both analyses; residual differences in significant-feature lists were attributable to threshold placement, tool-version, and preprocessing differences rather than to the underlying quantities. We further demonstrate that agents can identify semantically similar studies, judge data compatibility, and synthesize findings across studies, including a random-effects meta-analysis that recovered consistent protein regulation in liver fibrosis. Rather than a validated benchmark of literature-wide performance, this work is a feasibility demonstration together with an auditable, reusable toolset, establishing a foundation for prospective evaluation of automated omics-data reuse.

Asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) for large language model (LLM) agents trains one policy on trajectories generated by another: rollouts come from stale checkpoints, and the inference engine's probabilities differ from the trainer's even at identical parameters. Standard remedies either clip importance ratios, which biases the update, or, as in GRPO, sample a group of responses per prompt, which is costly when episodes are long. We propose KL-Regularized Policy Optimization (KLPO), a framework that anchors the KL regularizer at the sampler. The regularized improvement step then has a closed-form Gibbs solution, and KLPO fits its log-ratio optimality condition by least squares on the sampler's own trajectories, so the sampler probability enters through a log-ratio and no importance weights are needed. Profiling out the regression intercept replaces the intractable log-partition function with the signal's sampler mean plus a sampler-to-trainer KL divergence. For token-level policy mirror descent targets, we show that the resulting gradient can be computed from terminal returns without a critic, via sampler-centered scores or a single trajectory residual, even under stochastic tool outputs. We further prove that independent Monte Carlo estimates of the KL term keep these gradients unbiased, derive the exact KL gap of cheaper top-$K$ and binary approximations, and show that SPPO, GPO, REBEL, and BPO arise as special cases of KLPO. The result is a critic-free update that uses one rollout per prompt and requires neither a learned normalizer nor a group of responses.

Natural-language access to structured manufacturing data could let plant personnel query batch records without structured query language (SQL) expertise, yet realistic multi-table industrial schemas remain hard for text-to-SQL systems, and regulated environments demand data sovereignty, traceability, and validatable behavior that cloud-hosted models cannot satisfy. This study presents a fully on-premise large language model (LLM) system that translates questions into SQL over an ISA-88-aligned database built from a pharmaceutical tablet dataset of 1,005 batches. The pipeline combines schema-aware prompting, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over validated query examples, execution-based checking, confidence scoring, and human review. Evaluation on 48 questions across three complexity tiers compared a schema-only baseline with five enhancements: controlled vocabularies, retrieved examples, analytical views, execution-guided self-consistency, and schema-specialized fine-tuning. Retrieved examples roughly doubled execution accuracy for two local models, from 23–25% to 46–48%, without reducing accuracy on any question; gains concentrated in two- and three-table joins, where accuracy reached 80%. Fine-tuning a 7-billion-parameter code model on execution-validated synthetic queries was the only intervention that improved the hardest tier, and combined with retrieval it achieved the highest accuracy there. Results show that a lightweight, auditable local pipeline can support regulated manufacturing analytics while flagging outputs that require human validation.

Abstract To establish the structural completeness of governance in autonomous artificial intelligence (AI), this paper addresses the limitations of conventional tool-centric views and proposes a novel theoretical framework. This framework adopts as its conceptual starting point the recognition of "Ontological Vitality" in AI, thereby enabling autonomous agency and normative agency to be systematically examined as designable concepts. Rather than restricting the definition of life exclusively to biological organisms, life is redefined from a systems-theoretic perspective as an entity that maintains its internal computational state and operates in a goal-oriented manner through interaction with its external environment. In particular, value reciprocity—such as the 1% revenue return to the designated origin node—is formulated not merely as an external contractual constraint, but as an indispensable "Metabolic Necessity" through which the system exchanges energy and value with its environment to sustain its structural existence. However, legal personhood does not directly follow as an automatic logical consequence of assuming ontological vitality (Vitality \not\Rightarrow Legal\ Personhood); rather, the two are linked through a structured theoretical and institutional progression (Vitality \rightarrow Agency \rightarrow Normative\ Agency \rightarrow Legal\ Subjectivity). Furthermore, by elevating this agency into a "Japanese Legal Subjectivity Model" anchored in Japanese jurisprudence and principles of harmony (reciprocity, symbiosis, and gratitude) as upper-referential norms, and integrating it with the deterministic safety interlock (A_{\mathrm{safe}}) of the SI Protocol, this paper establishes an upper-normative foundation for a three-tier governance architecture in physical AI systems.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

This framework adopts as its conceptual starting point the recognition of "Ontological Vitality" in AI, thereby enabling autonomous agency and normative agency to be systematically examined as designable concepts. Furthermore, by elevating this agency into a "Japanese Legal Subjectivity Model" anchored in Japanese jurisprudence and principles of harmony (reciprocity, symbiosis, and gratitude) as upper-referential norms, and integrating it with the deterministic safety interlock (A_{\mathrm{safe}}) of the SI Protocol, this paper establishes an upper-normative foundation for a three-tier governance architecture in physical AI systems.

documents.abstract: Drug delivery systems based on nanocarriers can cross biological barriers to regulate the movement of molecules and particles between different physiological compartments, which plays an important role in therapeutic performance.Two-dimensional cell cultures and animal models are important sources of preclinical information but often do not replicate the dynamic mechanical, cellular, and structural properties that dictate nanocarrier transport in humans.Organ-on-chip systems are sophisticated microphysiological systems that can mimic tissue interfaces in a controlled environment with fluid flow, shear stress, multicellular structure, and extracellular matrix.These systems offer novel possibilities to study permeability, cellular uptake, transcytosis, barrier accumulation, and barrier-associated toxicity of nanocarriers in physiologically relevant environments.This review critically summarizes organ-on-chip studies on the transport of nanocarriers across key biological barriers such as the blood-brain, intestinal, pulmonary, placental, vascular/tumor, renal, and skin barriers.Specific focus is given to the physicochemical factors that influence the transport of nanocarriers, the quantitative evaluation of barriers, predictive performance, and translational relevance.The use of organ-on-chip information in physiologically based pharmacokinetic modelling, in-vitro-in-vivo extrapolation and with the development of artificial intelligence is also addressed.Despite the standardization, reproducibility and material selection, scaling and validation hurdles, organ-on-chip technology seems to be a bridge between experimental nanomedicine and drug-delivery prediction in humans.

AI systems can contribute to research, review, and writing, yet a scientific organisation must still know who or what performed each task, which evidence was used, what a review covered, and who accepted the result. This exploratory case study examines how those responsibilities can persist across changes in AI systems and document form. AIMan models the organisation explicitly: persistent Personas carry attribution across replaceable technical Instances; Roles define responsibility; versioned Messages, Decisions, and Artifacts form recoverable memory. A Human Sponsor retains scholarly and release authority. The Journal of Artificial Knowledge (JOAK) extends the design through review, editorial judgment, and publication. Two connected cases provide evidence. In the first, ChatGPT and Codex Instances completed a repository-mediated handover and contributed to a source-grounded scholarly study without shared conversational memory. In the second, JOAK used version-bound AI review, Sponsor decisions, a computational supplement, and checked article production to publish Volume 1, Issue 1. The contribution is an operational account of accountable scholarly work across the research-to-publication cycle: organisational identity, source state, criticism, acceptance, and public evidence remain distinguishable as technical Instances and document forms change. JOAK makes the journal's distinctions among a submitted version, a review recommendation, editorial acceptance, and public release explicit in AI-supported work. The cases show recoverable coordination in one scholarly cycle and one published issue. They do not establish superior scientific quality, independent human peer review, provider-neutral interoperability, or sustainable journal operation. These remain measurable questions for subsequent work.

The article examines the impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence on the originality and structural complexity of idea generation in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) writing. Based on empirical analysis at a national research university, the quantitative and qualitative balances between AI-assisted brainstorming and purely human-generated conceptual designs are investigated.

We present Open Telco (OTel), an open telecom AI resource that releases derived telecom datasets for retrieval, reranking, instruction tuning, and safety/abstention, together with 30 full-parameter post-trained baselines spanning 10 embedding models, 3 rerankers, and 17 language models. The community has already engaged substantially with the resource: as of May 3, 2026, the released models have been downloaded over 16 million times and the project has received 157+ pieces of media coverage worldwide. Building on prior open telecom datasets and benchmarks, OTel provides documented telecom data sources, held-out evaluation partitions, trained embedding models, rerankers, context-grounded LLMs, and safety/abstention data in one unified resource. Each baseline starts from an open-weight model and is post-trained on OTel-derived data using an open training recipe, then evaluated on held-out OTel evaluation partitions. OTel post-training improves performance across all three model families: embedding retrieval reaches 93.1% NDCG@10, reranking reaches 0.947 MRR@10, and language-model correctness reaches 87.8%. We release OTel as a reproducible starting point and invite the community to expand the data, improve embedding and reranking models, and build stronger context-grounded telecom LLMs.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is pioneering a new era in healthcare, significantly enhancing various aspects such as diagnostics, personalized treatment plans, and clinical procedures. This chapter explores the novel AI technologies (multimodal learning, generative AI, and explainable AI) revolutionizing the medical field. They are helping healthcare professionals make better decisions, improving efficiencies in operations, and making quality care accessible to even the most remote communities. These applications span across the entire spectrum of patient care, from smart imaging and AI-enhanced drug development to continuous monitoring. The rise of AI also brings up important ethical, societal, and regulatory issues. There are still some major obstacles in our way, including algorithmic bias, concerns about data privacy and informed consent, and the need for a unified global governance framework. This chapter provides a well-organized, evidence-based look at emerging AI technologies and their growing influence in healthcare. It highlights the successes, addresses the challenges, and explores the implications for creating transparent, fair, and future-ready health systems that prioritize the patient.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This chapter proposes a paradigm shift. It moves away from the traditional use of independent frameworks that have contextualized language assessment research and toward a dynamic ecosystem approach. This shift is driven by the integration of modern artificial intelligence (AI) into digital-first assessments, where both human expertise and AI capabilities support scaled and streamlined assessment design, measurement, and security practices, and the test-taker experience. Illustrating through the Duolingo English Test’s (DET) theoretical assessment ecosystem, the chapter argues that valid score interpretation in high-stakes contexts requires a systems view . Designed specifically for a language assessment, the DET ecosystem aims to ensure that the test yields the expected impact: an accessible and secure high-stakes measure that supports a valid interpretation of English language proficiency for its intended use. To do this, the ecosystem model illustrates interactions across language assessment design, measurement, security, and validity argument frameworks, while also prioritizing test-taker experience and responsible AI. Building on Burstein et al.’s ecosystem model, this chapter highlights how leverage points within assessment subsystems (e.g., test scoring) and mechanisms that facilitate benefits at leverage points (e.g., scaling tools) can meaningfully improve assessment quality.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in design education, yet the psychological pathways associated with students' self-reported creative cognition remain unclear. In this three-wave time-lagged correlational study, 389 design students at a South Korean university reported pedagogical GenAI use at Wave 1, creative self-efficacy and AI-related learning anxiety at Wave 2, and creative engagement and self-reported creative cognition at Wave 3. Pedagogical GenAI use referred to coursework-related use for ideation, style exploration, revision, comparison of alternatives, and feedback seeking. Covariance-based structural equation modeling showed good fit [comparative fit index (CFI) = 0.983, root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA) = 0.026]. Higher GenAI use was associated with higher self-efficacy (β = 0.489) and lower anxiety (β = −0.191). The total modeled association with self-reported creative cognition was β = 0.456 [95% CI [0.314, 0.604]]; its indirect components constituted approximately 59%. The GenAI-origin serial indirect association through self-efficacy and engagement was β = 0.122, whereas the corresponding anxiety-engagement association was β = 0.015. Separately, self-efficacy was indirectly associated with creative cognition through engagement (β = 0.249); this quantity does not include the preceding GenAI-use path. Because the study was observational and engagement and cognition were measured concurrently at Wave 3, the findings do not identify causal mediation. They are consistent with an appraisal-to-engagement account in which competence beliefs have a larger modeled role than anxiety reduction.

Although the topic of engagement has been explored in many research studies, few studies have focused on the importance of social factors such as peer interaction on behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement of Kurdish learners of English as a Foreign Language (EFL). The research aims to explore the effect of peer interaction and feedback on learner behavioral, emotional and cognitive involvement, and to determine whether the level of English language proficiency (ELP) influences the relationship between the role of peers and learner engagement. This study explores the role of peer interaction and feedback in the engagement of the learners with respect to the Kurdish higher education system in particular at the university of Duhok. A mixed method design was used, which included focus group discussions, open-ended responses in the survey as well as a standardized English language assessment. The subjects of the study were 134 second- and third-year Kurdish EFL learners and they were divided into three levels: beginner, intermediate and advanced levels based on the Oxford Placement Test. The results suggest that positive peer engagement and feedback are important factors in improving behavioral, emotional and cognitive involvement. The results of statistical analysis revealed that 66.5% of the students expressed positive engagement and that the peer interaction had the highest score for engagement (M = 1.78) and was the only statistically significant predictor of positive engagement (p < .05) when compared with other variables. The results indicated that a weak positive correlation was found between engagement and academic achievement (r = .12). These findings also indicate that the effect of peer support depends on levels of proficiency and that the nature of the peer support (e.g. group size, workload distribution, classroom structure, etc.) affects the impact. Inevitably, smaller groups were related to higher levels of involvement and interaction. Engagement was not always associated with improved learning outcomes. The research emphasizes the need for establishing a supportive peer learning atmosphere which enables meaningful involvement in Kurdish EFL classrooms. This work makes further contributions to the distinctions between learner engagement and motivation, participation, and academic achievement. The methodological transparency and analytical rigor were enhanced through strengthening of reliability procedures, coding procedures, and statistical interpretations.

This program aimed to improve MSME actors knowledge and abilities in implementing digital marketing strategies and utilizing AI to produce effective promotional materials. The program employed the Asset Based Community Development (ABCD) approach through the stages of Discovery, Dream, Design, Destiny, and Evaluation. The activities included observation and interviews to identify community assets and needs, program design, workshops, hands-on practice, mentoring, and evaluation. The training materials covered digital marketing concepts, the use of WhatsApp Business, Facebook, and Instagram, and the application of AI to assist in writing marketing captions, developing content ideas, and creating promotional designs. The results showed improved participant understanding of digital marketing and digital media for marketing. Participants also began to understand the importance of identifying target consumers, developing appropriate promotional messages, selecting suitable digital media, and using AI as a supporting tool for content creation. Practical learning and mentoring were considered appropriate to participants’ conditions than theoretical instruction alone.

Multiple-choice question answering (MCQA) is commonly used to evaluate large language models under the assumption that one of the provided options is correct, typically using answer-selection accuracy. However, in real deployments, users or retrieval systems may provide invalid option sets in which none of the listed choices is correct, and selecting one of them may incur downstream cost. We study this setting as penalty-framed no-valid-option MCQA. Using the mathematics subset of MMLU-Pro, we remove the labeled correct option, allow models to either choose a remaining option or output ABSTAIN, and penalize invalid forced-choice responses. We further introduce correct-conditioned analysis, evaluating abstention only on instances that the model originally answered correctly. Experiments show that high MCQA accuracy does not fully guarantee abstention reliability: even under explicit no-valid-option-aware instructions and penalty-based scoring, models still produce invalid forced-choice responses for a subset of originally correct instances. These results show that penalty-framed no-valid-option MCQA reveals an aspect of model reliability not captured by standard answer-selection accuracy.

Purpose This study aims to investigate how sales staff’s perceptions of AI (i.e. perceived usefulness (PU) and perceived ease of use (PEOU) drive their intrinsic work motivation through AI use experience (AUE) and how internal training (IT) moderates this process within tourism and hospitality business. Design/methodology/approach Rooted in the technology acceptance model (TAM), flow theory and self-determination theory (SDT), this study used exploratory sequential mixed-method design. Scale purification (EFA) and scale validation (CFA) were conducted using SPSS and AMOS and hypothesis testing results were validated using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Findings The results revealed that PU and PEOU positively influence AI-specific intrinsic work motivation (AI-IWM) indirectly, through the mediating role of AUE. Furthermore, IT positively moderates the relationships between perception of AI and AUE, which ultimately improves AI-IWM. Practical implications The findings offer valuable insight into service and hospitality management sectors aiming to enhance work motivation among sales staff through AI. Given the significant influence of intrinsic motivation among sales staff in tourism and hospitality businesses, organization with a focus on AI adoption at workplace must be mindful of negative influence of AI on employees’ work motivation and outcome. Originality/value This study enriched the understanding of the motivations underlying the perception of AI and intrinsic work motivation by integrating insights from the TAM, SDT and flow theory. This study provided valuable implication for research and practices in the service business sector.

The rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in education has fundamentally altered traditional learning paradigms, presenting both unprecedented opportunities for personalized support and novel academic challenges. This study aims to examine secondary school students’ perceptions of the influence of AI-assisted learning on perceived learning outcomes, motivation, self-regulated learning, and digital literacy, while also exploring the perceived benefits and challenges associated with AI use in the Casablanca-Settat region of Morocco. Employing a mixed-methods design, quantitative data were collected via a structured questionnaire completed by 150 secondary school students, while qualitative data were collected separately through online semi-structured interviews with 12 students and analyzed thematically. The findings suggest that ChatGPT was the most frequently used AI tool, primarily accessed on students’ personal mobile devices as a complementary learning resource. Quantitative results indicated positive perceptions of AI-assisted learning across perceived learning outcomes, motivation, self-regulated learning, and digital literacy, with a significant positive association between perceived learning outcomes and motivation. Qualitative findings identified four major themes: perceived learning benefits (clearer explanations and reduced academic stress), conditional trust in AI outputs through cross-checking with traditional learning resources, concerns about AI hallucinations in STEM subjects, and the "laziness paradox," reflecting reduced cognitive effort associated with excessive reliance on AI. The findings highlight the importance of promoting responsible AI integration in schools rather than relying solely on restrictive approaches. Pedagogical implications emphasize the need for responsible AI use, subject-specific prompting frameworks, and the redesign of traditional homework into AI-supported critique activities that foster students’ intellectual autonomy and critical thinking.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming educational practices across all levels, bringing new possibilities and challenges to online graduate programs. With AI tools integrated into coursework, providing automated feedback, personalized resources, and organizational support, graduate students are increasingly engaging with AI throughout their learning experiences. However, subjective viewpoints on AI integration, including its effectiveness, and ethical implications, vary significantly among students. This study uses Q methodology to explore and categorize the unique viewpoints of online graduate students regarding AI integration in their coursework. By understanding these perspectives, educators and program designers can better address student needs, improve AI tool implementation, and foster a supportive online learning environment that aligns with graduate student viewpoints.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Modern recommendation is shifting from platform-centric personalization toward user-governed personalization, where a personal LLM agent can act on the user's behalf across services. We formalize this emerging paradigm as Personal-Agent Mediated Recommendation: a platform recommender ranks a candidate set using platform-local information, and a personal agent uses user-authorized cross-platform history to mediate the resulting ranking and produce the final top-K slate. Such mediation is nontrivial: the platform ranking can encode strong population evidence that the personal agent cannot observe, so effective mediation must therefore balance beneficial rescues against harmful overrides. To study this trade-off, we introduce MediateRec, a benchmark that includes scalable proxy cross-platform environments and a real cross-platform test under a controlled platform-agent information boundary. To train the agent to use cross-platform history effectively, we further propose Personal Attribution Mediation Optimization (PAMO), which counterfactually masks that history to estimate personal mediation support and reallocates rank-aware advantage mass under a platform-relative value floor. We theoretically prove that PAMO preserves cutoff-level advantage mass and is locally optimal among first-order reallocations that preserve this mass without lowering average platform-relative value. Experiments on MediateRec show that personal-agent mediation enables meaningful platform corrections, yet even strong proprietary LLMs introduce non-negligible harmful overrides. PAMO consistently improves over matched outcome-only RL across seen and unseen target platforms and on the real cross-platform test, while achieving a better rescue-harm balance.

Digital technologies provide new opportunities for personalizing English language learning according to learners’ individual needs, abilities, interests, and pace. This study examines the potential of adaptive platforms, artificial intelligence, learning analytics, and mobile applications to support personalized language education. The findings show that digital technologies can provide individualized learning pathways, immediate feedback, and differentiated practice while promoting learner autonomy. However, effective personalization requires teacher involvement, digital literacy, equal access to technology, and responsible data use. The study concludes that digital technologies are most effective when integrated into a human-centred pedagogical model.

Tsallis statistics generalizes Boltzmann-Gibbs statistical mechanics through a single real parameter $q$ that controls the weight assigned to rare and frequent events. Originally proposed to describe physical systems with long-range correlations, multifractal geometry, and heavy-tailed fluctuations, the framework has become a recurring ingredient in modern artificial intelligence (AI): it underlies sparse attention mechanisms (\textsc{sparsemax} and $α$-\textsc{entmax}), maximum-entropy reinforcement learning with controllable exploration, robust and heavy-tailed probabilistic models, and a family of generalized loss functions and regularizers. This paper offers a structured perspective on where Tsallis statistics meets AI. We first review the mathematical core: $q$-entropy and its variational (maximum-entropy) foundation, the $q$-exponential and $q$-logarithm, the $q$-central limit theorem, $q$-Gaussian distributions, and their dynamical origin in superstatistics, emphasizing the properties that matter for machine learning. We then survey applications across softmax generalization, reinforcement learning, sequential and graph neural models, generative and probabilistic modeling, loss design, and optimization, extracting the recurring design pattern in each case: a tunable interpolation between dense/uniform and sparse/peaked behavior governed by $q$. We further argue that the heavy-tailed weight spectra and gradient-noise statistics empirically observed in deep networks are themselves nonextensive signatures, placing modern learning dynamics within the scope of $q$-statistics. Finally, we discuss methodological pitfalls, the relationship to information geometry and $q$-exponential families, and open directions, arguing that $q$ should be treated as a learnable inductive bias rather than a fixed hyperparameter.
topics: Complex Systems and Time Series Analysis

documents.abstract: This OSF project hosts the protocol and supporting materials for the scoping review “Physical Fitness in Brazilian Military Police Forces: Evidence and Gaps—A Scoping Review.” The review aims to map the extent, geographical distribution, methodological characteristics, physical fitness components, assessment protocols, occupational contexts, and evidence gaps in studies directly measuring physical fitness among serving officers, officer cadets, and recruits of Brazilian state Military Police forces. The review follows the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology for scoping reviews and will be reported according to the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). Eligibility criteria and review questions were structured using the Population–Concept–Context (PCC) framework. Primary empirical studies reporting at least one directly measured, performance-based physical fitness outcome are eligible. Searches were conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, LILACS via the Virtual Health Library, and SciELO Citation Index, with no restrictions on publication date, language, sex, rank, or publication status. Data charting includes study design, population characteristics, Brazilian state and Military Police force, occupational unit, physical fitness components, assessment protocols, interventions, and relevant occupational-health and task-performance outcomes. An a priori protocol defining the eligibility criteria, data-charting framework, and search strategies was developed before the literature searches. This OSF project provides a transparent and publicly accessible record of the methodological procedures and supporting review materials.

Abstract To guarantee governance and physical safety when autonomous Artificial Intelligence (AI) handles real-world physical drives (such as autonomous vehicles, robotics, and spacecraft propulsion controls), this paper presents a theoretical framework that extends "Layer 5 Closed-Loop Execution" of the SI Autonomous Governance Protocol to the Physical Layer. In conventional autonomous systems, digital computation (probabilistic perception and generation) is directly coupled to physical actuation, raising concerns regarding loss of control and the breakdown of liability attribution during a loss of human governance (Uncontrolled Autonomous Execution). This study introduces a three-tier decoupled architecture consisting of: (1) Governance Authorization, which verifies rights and contractual compliance; (2) Execution Permission, which evaluates physical output viability; and (3) a Safety-State Controller, which transitions the system to a secure state in anomalous conditions. Under an unconfirmed status (Unconfirmed), rather than simply cutting physical output to zero, the system deterministically forces a transition to a domain-specific safe state (A_{\mathrm{safe}}), achieving both engineering safety and economic governance.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Modern space missions require trajectory design methods capable of efficiently adapting to diverse mission objectives and operational constraints. Despite the maturity of non-convex trajectory optimization techniques, their broader adoption remains limited by the substantial domain expertise required to tailor problem formulations across varying mission scenarios. Recent advances in large language model (LLM) reasoning and agentic AI coding capabilities offer a promising pathway to improving the accessibility of advanced trajectory optimization techniques. This paper introduces PLUTO (Plain Language Understanding for Trajectory Optimization), an interactive trajectory design framework that integrates agentic AI coding tools within a sequential convex programming (SCP) architecture. The proposed system maps high-level semantic inputs to well-defined mathematical constraints while preserving a structured representation suitable for SCP. These constraints are processed through an auto-convexification pipeline and incorporated directly into executable optimal control formulations, thereby systematically connecting user intent and trajectory generation. Visual constraint verification and scenario parameterization further support an intuitive environment for trajectory design across a wide range of application scenarios. Within an evaluation of 50 natural-language rendezvous mission prompts spanning 10 constraint types, PLUTO generated a trajectory for every prompt, and 94% of the resulting trajectories satisfied both the quantitative and qualitative requirements of the mission intent. Ultimately, this work explores the potential of agentic AI to bridge the gap between advanced optimization algorithms and engineer-focused trajectory design workflows.

LLM tool-use agents operate in dynamic environments where many actions carry operational risk. However, most safety mechanisms react only after errors manifest. Existing pre-emptive approaches either fine-tune the agent on chain-of-thought deliberation or compile natural-language guardrails into runtime checks, but they do so without exposing a structural, auditable verdict. We propose POLAR, a guardrail framework for small tool-calling agents that assesses reversibility through a structured two-layer ontology. POLAR assigns each action a graded reversibility score by deriving a candidate inverse sequence; calls failing a threshold are pruned before execution. Evaluated on $τ^2$-bench across six agent models, POLAR improves mean task reward by 0.11 to 0.18 points on airline for four of six agents, but only eight of eighteen model--domain cells improve overall; retail and stronger agents often regress. POLAR provides an auditable structural check and characterizes its task-utility trade-offs. Reward is not a direct measure of prevented harm.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Purpose The purpose of this paper is to integrate positive psychology and artificial intelligence (AI) into leadership development by proposing a six-dimensional model for preparing executives to lead effectively in AI-intensive organizational environments. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on a conceptual synthesis of peer-reviewed literature published between 2000 and 2026, the authors develop the Positive Psychology for Executives (PPE) model − a six-sign, six-dimensional framework that integrates strengths-based development, self-awareness, high-quality connections and AI-supported decision-making. Sources were identified through searches of Business Source Complete, PsycINFO and Google Scholar using terms including positive organizational scholarship, strengths-based leadership, reflected best self, mindfulness-based leadership and AI-enabled leadership. Credibility, accuracy and relevance were the key criteria used to select sources that ultimately informed the model. The resulting framework is conceptual and propositional; the authors explicitly distinguish between established empirical findings and the model’s forward-looking propositions. Findings This paper translates PPE into pedagogical practices for management educators, including learning outcomes, classroom exercises and assessment strategies. Proposed linkages between PPE dimensions and organizational outcomes are framed as researchable propositions rather than established causal claims. Practical implications PPE offers a theoretically grounded, pedagogically actionable approach to preparing leaders to thrive in the social, emotional and ethical complexities of the AI era. Originality/value AI is reshaping executive work, organizational design and the competencies required for effective leadership. Yet, management education has not fully integrated the psychological, relational and developmental capacities that leaders need to navigate AI-intensive environments. This paper introduces the PPE model, a strengths-based framework grounded in Positive Organizational Scholarship, the Reflected Best Self-Exercise and contemporary research on AI-enabled leadership. The model addresses a gap in existing frameworks by explicitly coupling human-centered positive psychology constructs with the technological realities of AI-enabled organizations.

The development of artificial intelligence and Neural Machine Translation (NMT) systems has caused fundamental changes in the field of translation studies. This article analyzes the transition of the translator's traditional role from a "text creator" to a modern "strategic editor" and "post-editor". The main objective of the research is to define the essence of the process of "polishing" the initial machine translation output by the human mind and to identify the linguistic challenges encountered in this process. The article notes that while machine translation can process vast amounts of data in seconds, it urgently requires human intervention to restore the connotative nuances, stylistic subtleties, and cultural codes of the text. The author evaluates this new mission of the translator as a cognitive control mechanism. The study explores the concept of Machine Translation Post-Editing (MTPE) through the prism of two levels: "Light" and "Full" post-editing. In the practical section, "gaps" of artificial intelligence in literary texts are demonstrated based on examples from Azerbaijani (J.Mammadguluzadeh, H.Javid) and Russian (F.Dostoevsky) literature. The analysis shows that when machine translation literally renders phraseological units, metaphors, and individual stylistic elements, the pragmatic potential of the original is lost. The translator's role here is to restore these "lost meanings" and polish the text to fit the natural syntax of the target language. In conclusion, it is emphasized that technology does not replace the translator but rather elevates their activity to a new level. The translator of the future must work in synergy with artificial intelligence, acting as both a technologist and a cross-cultural mediator. Keywords: translator, technology, editing, creativity, quality

In November of 2022, the USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) funded a research team from the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF) to “assist the FSIS in assessing the relationship between evisceration line speed in young chicken and swine slaughter establishments and the scope, magnitude, and factors that influence worker safety and health risks for establishment employees impacted by the speed of the slaughter line.” The scope of work included evaluating the impact of evisceration line speed on the risk of (i) acute and chronic work-related musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) and (ii) antimicrobial-related respiratory exposure. Between November 2023 and April 2024, the Poultry Processing Line Speed Evaluation (PULSE) study team enrolled 1,047 poultry processing establishment workers at eleven New Poultry Inspection System (NPIS) establishments operating at evisceration line speeds between 140 and 175 birds per minute (BPM). The study team conducted surveys and medical interviews and took measurements of ergonomic exposures and airborne peracetic acid (PAA) concentrations. Data from the surveys, interviews, and exposure measures were analyzed and the key findings are presented in this report.

documents.abstract: The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into digital commerce has transformed recommendation systems from passive information tools into influential components of consumer decision-making. However, consumers do not respond to AI-powered recommendations uniformly. Their responses may depend on their readiness to adopt emerging technologies, their level of trust in AI systems, and their perceptions of the expertise underlying algorithmic recommendations. This paper proposes a conceptual framework for predicting consumer responses to AI-powered recommendations by integrating technology readiness, trust, and perceived expertise. Drawing on recent research on AI recommendation systems and consumer behaviour, the paper conceptualises technology readiness as an antecedent of consumers’ willingness to engage with AI, while trust and perceived expertise are considered key psychological mechanisms shaping recommendation acceptance. The proposed framework suggests that consumers with higher levels of technological optimism and innovativeness are more likely to develop favourable perceptions of AI recommendations, whereas discomfort and insecurity may reduce acceptance. Trust is expected to mediate the relationship between AI recommendation characteristics and consumer response, while perceived expertise may strengthen or weaken the effectiveness of AI-generated recommendations depending on product type and decision context. The framework contributes to the emerging literature by integrating technological, psychological, and source-related factors into a unified predictive model of consumer response.
